metadata.title: CNN vs RNN vs LSTM - When and Why to Use Each

beats.title: The Question
beats.narration_text: Hi. This is Sanjiv. Today we shall discuss CNNs, RNNs, and LSTMs, and when and why to use each. We will follow how they handle information, work through small examples, and turn those differences into practical choices.

beats.title: The Big Picture
beats.narration_text: Choose a fit for the task. Local patterns, sequence order, and memory requirements shape the decision. An LSTM is a type of recurrent network. Here, when we compare it with an RNN, we mean a basic, ungated RNN.

show.event: Older hesitant overview: replace “a universal winner” with “a fit for the task” in “Choose a universal winner.” Final sentence: “Choose a fit for the task.” Three compact context cards.

beats.title: Three Ways to Handle Information
beats.narration_text: Imagine three jobs: finding a defect in an image, following a sensor stream, and remembering an earlier event when interpreting a later reading. These suggest different ways to connect a network. The data format alone does not decide which model will work best.

show.event: Reveal image grid, ordered signal, and delayed cue separately, then align them. No accuracy bars.

beats.title: CNN: Reuse a Local Detector
beats.narration_text: A convolutional neural network applies the same learned filter at different locations. Each application examines a local neighborhood. Sharing weights lets a useful pattern detector work across the image. Deeper layers combine local features into larger patterns.

show.event: Slide one highlighted 3-by-3 kernel across a small image; build feature-map cells. Show shared weights once.

beats.title: A Tiny Convolution
beats.narration_text: Take five values: one, two, three, four, five. Apply a filter with weights one, zero, and negative one. Each three-value window produces negative two. This is the cross-correlation operation commonly called convolution in neural networks. The same filter also works along a time axis.

show.event: Animate a width-three window over [1,2,3,4,5], with filter [1,0,-1], producing [-2,-2,-2]. Label constructed example, stride one, no padding.

beats.title: When a CNN Fits
beats.narration_text: A CNN is a useful candidate when nearby values form recurring patterns: textures in images, or short motifs in signals. Stacking layers or using dilation expands the region each output can use. A shallow filter sees only its local window, so check the required context.

show.event: Image defects and waveform motifs, sequentially. Expand receptive-field brackets across stacked layers.

beats.title: RNN: Carry a State Forward
beats.narration_text: A basic recurrent neural network processes a sequence step by step. Each step combines the new input with the previous hidden state. That state is a learned summary of earlier inputs. The same update rule is reused through time, and changing the order can change the result.

show.event: Unroll three recurrent cells; reuse one weight label. State travels above input nodes; arrows avoid labels.

shot.visual_intent: Unroll three recurrent cells; reuse one weight label. State travels above input nodes; arrows avoid labels.

beats.title: A Tiny Recurrent Update
beats.narration_text: In a constructed one-unit example, combine the input with half the previous state, then apply tanh. Starting from zero, inputs one, zero, zero produce states about zero point seven six two, zero point three six three, and zero point one eight zero. Earlier information influences later steps.

show.event: Reveal h_t=tanh(x_t+0.5h_previous), h0=0. Input [1,0,0]; states approximately [.762,.363,.180]. Each state replaces the previous highlight.

shot.visual_intent: Reveal h_t=tanh(x_t+0.5h_previous), h0=0. Input [1,0,0]; states approximately [.762,.363,.180]. Each state replaces the previous highlight.

beats.title: Where a Basic RNN Struggles
beats.narration_text: Training sends gradients backward through those steps. Repeated transformations can make them shrink or grow. As a simple illustration, multiplying by one half ten times gives about one thousandth. A basic RNN can be a small baseline for short dependencies, but long-range learning can be difficult.

show.event: Backward gradient arrows through a long chain; illustrative factors 0.5 repeated ten times. Label illustration, not measured benchmark.

shot.visual_intent: Backward gradient arrows through a long chain; illustrative factors 0.5 repeated ten times. Label illustration, not measured benchmark.

beats.title: LSTM: Control the Memory
beats.narration_text: Long short-term memory networks add a cell state and learned gates. The forget gate controls retained memory, the input gate controls new content, and the output gate controls what reaches the hidden state. This structure helps gradients travel through time, but does not guarantee perfect memory.

show.event: Show cell-state path, then forget/input/output gates one at a time. Separate hidden-state output below.

shot.visual_intent: Show cell-state path, then forget/input/output gates one at a time. Separate hidden-state output below.

beats.title: One Gated Memory Update
beats.narration_text: Suppose the old cell value is zero point five. Retain eighty percent of it and add twenty percent of a candidate value of zero point three. The new cell value is zero point four six. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation; a trained LSTM learns its gate values.

show.event: Show c_new=f*c_old+i*g, then 0.8*0.5+0.2*0.3=0.46. Gates labeled supplied illustrative values; output gate shown only after calculation.

shot.visual_intent: Show c_new=f*c_old+i*g, then 0.8*0.5+0.2*0.3=0.46. Gates labeled supplied illustrative values; output gate shown only after calculation.

beats.title: When an LSTM Fits
beats.narration_text: Consider an LSTM when useful context must persist across many steps and recurrent processing suits the application. Sensor histories and sequence labeling are examples. The gates add parameters and computation compared with a basic RNN at the same hidden width. Test whether the added capacity earns its cost.

show.event: Delayed cue moves along timeline to later decision; show state and bounded-memory icon. No claim that delay alone selects winner.

shot.visual_intent: Delayed cue moves along timeline to later decision; show state and bounded-memory icon. No claim that delay alone selects winner.

beats.title: Compare the Constraints
beats.narration_text: CNN windows can be computed in parallel within a layer. Recurrent steps depend on earlier states, which limits parallelism across time. For live prediction, prevent future information from entering the model: use causal convolutions or a forward-only recurrent design. Measure latency on the actual deployment hardware.

show.event: Three sparse comparison rows revealed independently: locality; recurrent state; gated state. Parallel-window illustration versus step dependency.

shot.visual_intent: Three sparse comparison rows revealed independently: locality; recurrent state; gated state. Parallel-window illustration versus step dependency.

beats.title: Choose Through an Experiment
beats.narration_text: For image defects, start by testing a CNN. For a short stream, a basic RNN can establish a recurrent baseline. For delayed context, test an LSTM and a temporal CNN. Compare against a simple baseline using the same task metric, suitable validation split, and deployment budget.

show.event: Three scenario cards sequentially: image defect→CNN candidate; short stream→basic RNN baseline; delayed context→LSTM candidate. Then validation split schematic.

shot.visual_intent: Three scenario cards sequentially: image defect→CNN candidate; short stream→basic RNN baseline; delayed context→LSTM candidate. Then validation split schematic.

beats.title: The Verdict
beats.narration_text: These are starting points for experiments. Temporal CNNs can compete with recurrent networks on sequence tasks, and other architectures may also fit. Choose the connections that match the problem, then let held-out results, memory use, and latency determine whether that choice holds up.

beats.title: Your Turn
beats.narration_text: Compare a CNN, a basic RNN, and an LSTM for my dataset. Ask about input structure, required context, available labels, and latency. Propose a baseline and a validation plan. Use this prompt with a specific task. Look for a testable recommendation tied to your constraints.
